doc.title: Bill Goodwin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 28, 2025

chapter: Coming up on the L.A. scene
title: Dennis Budimir, Terry Gibbs at the Crescendo, and the 'bebop newspaper'
summary: Budimir's influence on Frisell, being hired at 19 by Terry Gibbs at the Crescendo owned by Gene Norman, his father's connections, and the nickname 'bebop Walter Winchell'.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Well Bud was already there. Dennis went there. Dennis Budimir, I don’t know if you know him, was a marvelous guitar player. Extremely creative. And was an influence on Bill Frisell, according to Bill anyway, Bill told me that. We made some records, home recordings that later came out and Bill being much younger than us he had heard them when he was young and he told me once he was extremely influenced by Dennis and those records, which was nice to hear you know. And so what happened — oh it’s still a blur — so much was going on and L.A. was just rife with things to do. Lots of gigs, lots of jam sessions, lots of rehearsals. So you know I started making my way but at 19 I got hired by Terry Gibbs to play with him, you know, Hollywood on Sunset Strip, The Crescendo. And The Crescendo was owned by Gene Norman who had a late night radio show in L.A. and played jazz, and he also had the Gene Norman Presents label and he had put out the “Dizzy Gillespie at the Shrine Auditorium,” a big band record which I loved, and he put out the first Clifford Brown/Max Roach record which I loved. And he was like my dad, a famous, at least locally, radio voice, and a wonderful voice. And of course I’d meet these people later on in life and they’d all say what an influence my father was on them, it was pretty nice to have that association. But it was really my sister and my mother who I think were more instrumental in my career. So my dad would take me out to hear music and stuff and he knew everybody. So you know within five minutes of coming to a club, you know we’d be sitting with the band.
I love that, sitting with the band. I have it from an inside source that you used to be known as the “bebop newspaper.”

Oh where’d you hear that? It was started as a — I think it was — I don’t know it could have been Dick Wittington my piano player friend, another part of our clique, Dick, or it was a piano player named Marty Harris that I played with a lot too and he used to call me, Dick called me the “bebop Walter Winchell.”
Oh. Well an acquaintance named Art Bailey gave me that little inside scoop.
Well yeah, that’s cool. I bet I told Art that.
